states.name: paragraph
states.gap: Sets ~1.6% wider on an identical 74px line pitch — 27.98px vs 27.53px per character advance — so leading drops from ~1.61 to ~1.59 em and the paragraph loses a word per line inside the same 1740px viewport (line 2 stops at 'and it was' vs A's 'and it was not', ending 113px from the right edge against A's 35px).
states.gapTheirs: Dirty rasterisation: 2,082 unique colours against B's 333, with ±1 RGB dither smeared across a ground that should be one flat value (only 37% of A's pixels are exactly #F7F7F7 vs B's 95%), and chromatic fringing on body stems measuring HSL-saturation up to 32/255 where B measures 0 — colour edges on ~23px logical monospace on a light field.
states.verdict: On the thing this piece is actually about, these two are the same page: identical #F7F7F7 ground, identical #191919 lit body, identical #C4C4C4 dim on the heading (1.63:1 contrast — barely there in both), identical 74px line pitch, identical 72px text-left with the marker hung at x≈20, and neither dims anything inside the paragraph. Nothing here lets a writer choose on focus behaviour, so the decision falls to how the page is put on glass, and A loses that: its 'flat' background isn't flat and its stems carry colour fringes, while B renders two values and stops. B's penalty is that it sets fatter for no gain — you buy 1.6% more glyph and pay a word off the end of every line.
secondary: Both show exactly two tiers (#191919 lit / #C4C4C4 dim) — no third shade on either side.
Both rest the '#' at the dim line's own ink (#C4C4C4), matching the heading text exactly in hex.

Marker weight differs and is not a colour matter: A's '#' carries 47% more ink than the heading's own 'L' (18.67 vs 12.68), B's carries 4% less (12.86 vs 13.35) — A's marker is bold with the heading, B's is regular against bold.
Neither frame contains a caret at all, so caret width, colour and blink are unjudgeable from these.
The 320px strip shows no window top or bottom, so the typewriter rest position cannot be read on either side.
The dim tier at #C4C4C4 on #F7F7F7 is 1.63:1 in both — the heading is close to invisible, not merely receded.
Right margin is unbalanced against the 72px left in both: A's longest line ends 35px from the edge, B's line 1 ends 68px from it.

states.name: dark-sentence-typewriter
states.gap: Leading is 74 device px (37 CSS px) against B's 76 px — ~1.65 vs ~1.71 line-height at an identical ~26.8px glyph advance. One CSS pixel per line, but over a 40-line session A's block is measurably tighter and the dim paragraphs pack denser than B's.
states.gapTheirs: A third dim tier the design does not have: the sentence following the caret's sentence is painted #888888 (4.9:1 on #1A1A1A) while the rest of the same wrapped line is #707070 (3.5:1) and the caret's sentence is #CCCCCC (10.8:1) — three brightnesses inside one line of text, 3,395px of a grey that appears nowhere else. A holds a clean two-step bright/dim.
states.verdict: B builds a halo around the focused sentence and it backfires on the line that matters most: 'beside it.' is lit, 'The door took both hands to open.' is a middling grey that reads as half-awake, and 'Outside, the wind' drops again — three greys, left to right, in one line. You end up asking which sentence you're actually in, which is the exact question focus mode exists to abolish. A answers it in one step: this sentence is on, everything else is off, one flat #707070 all the way down the page. B's one extra pixel of leading does not buy back a tier that makes you re-read your own line to find the caret.

Both dim tiers land on the same #707070 and both lit runs on #CCCCCC — the bright:dim luminance step is 3.09x in both
Focus scope matches: both light the sentence, not the paragraph, and both carry the lit run correctly across two wraps
